title: Worse, but unique: why a "refuted" strategy beats the popular one for startups
summary: Using chess openings as an analogy, Jason argues that an objectively worse but unusual strategy beats a popular, objectively better one, because opponents are prepared for the popular one and not for yours. Startups should fight on their own terms, pick an extreme difference, and accept that many customers won't want their game.

principles.text: Don't attack where the incumbent is strong; fight the competitive battle on your own terms.
principles.quote: A startup needs to fight the competitive battle on its own terms, not attack where the opponent is already strong.

principles.text: Popular strategies are the ones competitors have prepared against; a niche, 'refuted' one catches them unprepared.
principles.quote: exactly because the Queen's Gambit is popular, it's likely that your opponent has also studied it.

principles.text: Playing a different game on your own terms can make a 'worse' strategy better, even if your team, product and company are weaker.
principles.quote: Playing on your own terms changes the game. "Worse, but unique," is in fact "better."

principles.text: Be extreme in your difference, not merely different; one extreme trait is already powerful.
principles.quote: Even better than "different," is to be extreme in that difference.

principles.text: Competitors can't match an extreme choice, so they are definitionally not the best at your game.
principles.quote: All those competitors *cannot* play the game as well as you, because you picked something that was not only different, but extreme.

principles.text: Accept losing customers who don't want your game; the ones who do will see you as the best, and you can still win big in a large market.
principles.quote: The customers who *do* want to play your game, will see that you're the best in that game.
